title: Hamas Just Dissolved Its Government in Gaza. India Stayed Out of the Peace Plan — and Has Its Reasons.
excerpt: The militant group's symbolic move pressures Israel to act on a stalled US-brokered deal. India's refusal to join Trump's Board of Peace reflects a calculation that runs through 8.5 million NRIs in the Gulf.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Hamas dissolved its government in Gaza, signaling a shift towards a U.S.-backed committee.
  • India opted out of Trump's Board of Peace, balancing ties with Israel and support for Palestinians.
  • Over 8.5 million Indians in the Gulf rely on remittances, crucial for India's economy.
  • Israel continues military operations in Gaza, with over 1,059 deaths reported since the ceasefire.
  • Hamas retains control over security in Gaza, refusing to disarm until Israel halts military actions.
Hamas's Shift in Governance
›Hamas dissolved its de facto government in Gaza.
›Power to be transferred to a 15-member panel of technocrats.
›Hamas retains control over security and policing.
›Refuses to disarm until Israel stops military operations.
Hamas announced on Monday that it has dissolved its de facto government in Gaza, signalling its readiness to hand administrative power to a U.S.-backed committee of Palestinian technocrats — a move that puts pressure squarely on Israel to fulfil its side of a stalled peace plan, and raises pointed questions about India's deliberate absence from the process. The dissolution ends an oversight body that has governed Gaza's ministries for over a decade. Ismail Al-Thawabta, director of the Hamas government media office, said at a press conference in Gaza City that the head of the "Government Emergency Committee" had resigned and the body itself had been dissolved. ## What Hamas Is Giving Up — and What It Is Not The group said it is ready to transfer civilian administration to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), a 15-member panel of Palestinian technocrats created under President Donald Trump's Board of Peace. The committee's chief commissioner, Ali Shaath, a civil engineer and former Palestinian Authority official, said his team was ready to assume responsibility as soon as "necessary resources and enabling conditions" were in place. But Hamas made clear it is not giving up everything. The group said it would retain control over security and policing in parts of Gaza still under its authority, and its appointed ministry staff would remain. It has refused to disarm — a core requirement of the peace plan's second phase — until Israel halts military operations in the enclave. ![Gaza City — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/Images_of_war_23-25_from_Gaza%2C_by_Jaber_Badwen%2C_IMG_6315.jpg/3840px-Images_of_war_23-25_from_Gaza%2C_by_Jaber_Badwen%2C_IMG_6315.jpg) > **"More than 8.5 million Indian nationals live and work across the Gulf states, their remittances forming a critical pillar of India's economy."** Trump's Board of Peace said it "took note" of Hamas's announcement but would judge "actions, not promises," calling for full disarmament under the principle of "one authority, one law, and one weapon." ## Israel Has Not Responded There was no immediate comment from Israel, which controls more than 60 per cent of Gaza and has continued military operations since the fragile October ceasefire. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said last month he had ordered the seizure of 70 per cent of the enclave and suggested Israel could take more. Israeli airstrikes killed five people in Gaza on Monday — a couple in an apartment in Tel Al-Hawa and three others in strikes on a displacement tent and a vehicle in Khan Younis — medics said. At least 1,059 people have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire was signed on October 11, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health. Muhammad Shehada, a Gaza expert at the European Council on Foreign Relations, described Hamas's move as an attempt to "talk over Netanyahu's head" and appeal directly to Trump, calling it a "savvy move" — but one that likely comes too late. ![President Donald Trump — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/13/Official_Presidential_Portrait_of_President_Donald_J._Trump_%282025%29_%28cropped%29%282%29.jpg)
India's Strategic Position
›India has 8.5 million nationals in Gulf states.
›Remittances from the Gulf are vital for India's economy.
›India's absence from the peace board reflects complex geopolitical balancing.
›Participation could strain relationships with Gulf nations.
"Even if that bet pays off — even if Trump is convinced, and even if everything goes according to plan — Israel still has ultimate control over everything in Gaza," Shehada told CNN. ## Why India Stayed Away — and Why It Matters India has conspicuously declined to join Trump's Board of Peace, a decision that reflects New Delhi's careful balancing act between its deepening ties with Israel and the United States, its historic support for Palestinian self-determination, and its strategic relationships across the Arab world. A report by the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) described the board invitation as a "risky proposition," citing the absence of Palestinian political ownership, the bypassing of UN frameworks that India has traditionally supported, and commercial interests that could prioritise development projects over Palestinian rights. Former Indian diplomat and West Asia expert Ambassador Talmiz Ahmed was more blunt, calling India's participation an "absolute travesty" that would undermine the country's civilisational ethos and strategic autonomy. India's caution is not merely ideological. More than 8.5 million Indian nationals live and work across the Gulf states, their remittances forming a critical pillar of India's economy. Gulf governments — particularly the UAE, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar — have been closely watching how regional powers respond to the Gaza crisis. Aligning too closely with any single framework risks straining relationships that underpin energy security, trade corridors, and the safety of the Indian diaspora across the Middle East.
Gaza's Dire Situation
›Over 1,059 people killed in Gaza since the ceasefire.
›Nearly 2 million people displaced, living in tents or damaged buildings.
›UN accuses Israel of genocide, a claim Israel rejects.
The situation in Gaza remains dire. Nearly the entire population of two million has been displaced, most now living in tents or damaged buildings. A UN commission found in June that Israel was continuing to commit genocide against Palestinians — an accusation Israel rejected as "a political blood libel." For the millions of Indians in the Gulf and the broader diaspora watching from the US, UK, and Canada, the trajectory of the Gaza conflict is not abstract geopolitics. It shapes the stability of the region they live in, the energy prices their families pay, and the moral calculus of the democracies they call home.
